findings.title: A written, appointed horizon for settlement fate
findings.claim: 17:58 bounds a settlement's destruction-or-severe-punishment before Yawm al-Qiyamah and places that outcome in the Kitab as an inscription. The wider 15:4 says each destroyed town has a known kitab, while 18:59 joins destroyed towns to an appointed time for their destruction. Together these connections make the focus read as a settlement-level endpoint recorded within ordered time, rather than an isolated catastrophe.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries qaryah, transitive destruction, kitab, and masturan, with a before-Qiyamah limit. The wider 15:4 repeats the town-destruction and known-book relation; 18:59 joins destroyed towns to an appointed time. Their contact aligns the focus's inscription with a wider pattern of per-settlement records and appointed endpoints.
findings.reader_payoff: The settlement's fate becomes legible as a bounded entry in a wider record of civic outcomes, not only as a detached forecast of ruin.
findings.containment: This does not identify the same historical towns across the ayat, assert identical outcomes for all settlements, or resolve whether qaryah foregrounds the site or its people. Target morphology and lexical analysis are not supplied for the wider texts; the record-and-appointment relation is contextual, not a target-side root claim.

epistemic.reason: A trusted cross-run finding and an exact duplicate legacy reader claim are supported by supplied wider Arabic parallels, but the legacy support is non-citable and target-side morphology is absent.

findings.title: Removal, renewed settlement, and later gathering
findings.claim: A wider narrative sequence sets an attempted expulsion from the land beside the drowning of Pharaoh and his company, then commands the Children of Israel to settle the land and associates the Hereafter's promise with their later gathering as a multitude. As an analogue to 17:58, it distinguishes decisive removal from a later inhabited and gathered state.
findings.mechanism: 17:103 supplies the attempted expulsion and the drowning of the ruler and his company; 17:104 then supplies a command to settle the land and a future Hereafter gathering. These connect back to the focus's transitive destruction and its before-Qiyamah horizon, placing civic history and final assembly at different moments.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus's destructive horizon need not be conflated with final erasure: a wider narrative can place renewed settlement before a later collective gathering.
findings.containment: These verses concern Pharaoh and the Children of Israel, not a town identified in 17:58. They do not say the Israelites were displaced, do not describe a town's rebuilding, and do not prove that 17:104's gathering is identical in scope to the focus's Qiyamah.

epistemic.reason: The legacy retrospective is non-citable and its displacement gloss is narrowed; the supplied exact 17:103-104 Arabic supports the bounded narrative analogy.

findings.title: The settlement as a civic collective
findings.claim: The focus's qaryah can denote more than a place: the wider 29:31 explicitly places a town's people under its destruction. This makes a collective-inhabitants reading available for the settlement fate in 17:58, alongside the literal place reading.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries qaryah as a settlement; 29:31 names a qaryah and then explicitly refers to its people as the subject whose wrongdoing explains the announced destruction. That wider relation returns to the focus word and shifts the possible object from site alone to the people gathered there.
findings.reader_payoff: A settlement's fate can be heard as a fate of its civic body, not only as the loss of buildings or territory.
findings.containment: This is an available collective metonymy, not a claim that qaryah in 17:58 must mean inhabitants rather than the place. The target text supplies exact Arabic but no target morphology or lexical analysis; same-surah context cited by the legacy source is excluded from this global finding.

epistemic.reason: The legacy candidate is narrowed to its qaryah branch, and the wider 29:31 text independently supplies the collective-people trigger; target-side morphology remains unavailable.

findings.title: Community fate and personal accountability
findings.claim: The focus's community-level horizon does not erase personal accounting or make punishment without warning. The wider 17:13 gives each individual an open book at Yawm al-Qiyamah; 17:15 separates each person's guidance or error, forbids bearing another's burden, and says punishment follows the sending of a messenger; 7:164 places the same destroy-or-severely-punish alternative inside an exchange that keeps admonition meaningful.
findings.mechanism: The focus's named Day and Kitab contact with the individual book at 17:13, distinguishing a communal pre-Day inscription from personal accounting at the Day. The focus's severe-punishment branch then contacts 17:15's messenger-before-punishment limit and 7:164's repeated alternatives followed by a call to admonish, changing a bare fate forecast into a horizon that still includes personal responsibility and warning.
findings.reader_payoff: A universal settlement-level horizon can coexist with individual moral responsibility and meaningful admonition; the civic record is not a transferable sentence for every resident.
findings.containment: These connections do not specify the fate of every person in a particular town or say that all settlements receive the same outcome. The contexts are distinct passages, and their exact Arabic is supplied without target-side morphology or lexical analysis.

epistemic.reason: The reading is independently grounded in supplied exact target Arabic and direct contextual relations, but target morphology is absent and the links are contextual rather than target-side lexical proofs.

findings.title: Civic non-return and resurrection are distinct
findings.claim: The wider texts distinguish a destroyed settlement's social non-return from resurrection. 21:95 says the people of a destroyed qaryah do not return; 2:259 asks how a ruined town could be revived, then narrates the revival of a man after a hundred years and the restoration of an animal's bones, without saying that the town itself is rebuilt. Thus the focus's pre-Qiyamah settlement destruction does not deny resurrection of persons or guarantee restoration of the former civic body.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries qaryah and destruction. 21:95 returns through qaryah to the non-return of a destroyed settlement's people, while 2:259 contacts the destruction carrier with a town-level revival question and then a narrated individual revival. The different subjects keep civic reconstruction and resurrection from collapsing into one event.
findings.reader_payoff: A town's social non-return can stand alongside resurrection of persons; neither claim automatically entails the other.
findings.containment: 21:95 does not say that its people are not resurrected for judgment. 2:259 raises the town's revival but does not narrate its rebuilding; the explicit restoration signs concern the man and the animal. These contexts do not identify their towns with the focus settlement.

epistemic.reason: The supplied target Arabic and connection notes support the contextual contrast, but no target morphology is supplied and 2:259's town-level restoration remains an unanswered question in the narrated text.
